The '''Hilbert–Bernays paradox''' is a distinctive [[paradox]] belonging to the family of the [[list of self–referential paradoxes|paradoxes of reference]]. It is named after [[David Hilbert]] and [[Paul Bernays]].

{{TOC limit|3}}

==History==

The paradox appears in Hilbert and Bernays' ''[[Grundlagen der Mathematik]]'' and is used by them to show that a sufficiently strong consistent theory cannot contain its own reference functor.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hilbert|first1=David|last2=Bernays|first2=Paul|title=Grundlagen der Mathematik|date=1939|publisher=Springer|location=Berlin|pages=263–278}}</ref> Although it was largely unnoticed over the course of the 20th century, it has recently been rediscovered and appreciated for the distinctive difficulties it presents.<ref name="Priest2005">{{cite book|last1=Priest|first1=Graham|title=Towards Non-Being|date=2005|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=Oxford|pages=156–178}}</ref>

==Formulation==

Just as the [[semantics|semantic]] property of [[truth]] seems to be governed by the naive schema:

:(T) The sentence ′''P''′ is true if and only if ''P''

(where single quotes refer to the linguistic expression inside the quotes), the semantic property of reference seems to be governed by the naive schema:

:(R) If ''a'' exists, the referent of the name ′''a''′ is identical with ''a''

Let us suppose, however, that for every expression '''e''' in the language, the language also contains a name '''<e>''' for that expression, and consider a name '''h''' for (natural) numbers satisfying:

:(H) '''<h>''' is identical with ′(the referent of '''<h>''')+1′

Suppose that, for some number ''n'':

:(1) The referent of '''<h>''' is identical with ''n''

Then, surely, the referent of '''<h>''' exists, and so does (the referent of '''<h>''')+1. By (R), it then follows that:

:(2) The referent of ′(the referent of '''<h>''')+1′ is identical with (the referent of '''<h>''')+1

Therefore, by (H) and the principle of [[identity of indiscernibles|indiscernibility of identicals]], it is the case that:

:(3) The referent of '''h''' is identical with (the referent of '''h''')+1

But, by two more applications of the indiscernibility of identicals, (1) and (3) yield:

:(4) ''n'' is identical with ''n''+1

But (4) is absurd, since no number is identical with its successor.

==Solutions==

Since, given the [[diagonal lemma]], every sufficiently strong theory will have to accept something like (H),{{clarify|reason=Why should (1) be true, i.e. why should a number exist that satisfies the property h? For example, no natural number is designated by the name 'The number whose square is 2', but this isn't called a paradox.|date=May 2015}} absurdity can only be avoided either by rejecting the principle of naive reference (R) or by rejecting [[classical logic]] (which validates the reasoning from (R) and (H) to absurdity). On the first approach, typically whatever one says about the [[Liar paradox]] ''carries over smoothly'' to the Hilbert–Bernays paradox.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Keith Simmons|editor1-last=Beall|editor1-first=JC|title=Liars and Heaps|date=2003|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=Oxford|pages=230–252|chapter=Reference and Paradox}}</ref> The paradox presents instead ''distinctive difficulties'' for many solutions pursuing the second approach: for example, solutions to the Liar paradox that reject the [[law of excluded middle]] (which is ''not'' used by the Hilbert–Bernays paradox) have denied that there is such a thing as the referent of '''h''';<ref>{{cite book|last1=Field|first1=Hartry|title=Saving Truth from Paradox|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=Oxford|pages=291–293}}</ref> solutions to the [[Liar paradox]] that reject the [[law of noncontradiction]] (which is likewise ''not'' used by the Hilbert–Bernays paradox) have claimed that '''h''' refers to more than one object.<ref name="Priest2005"/>
